title: SimVLA: Attributing Gains in VLA Models Through Controlled Ablation
claim: One minimal model, deployed zero-shot on unseen scenes, completes many varied multi-stage manipulation tasks that require dexterity and semantic understanding.
layout: 8 rows by 6 columns grid, time left-to-right, task label per row
description: A dense gallery of real-robot rollout frames in an 8-row by 6-column grid. Each row is one task, labeled with rotated text at the left: store the dolls, arrange eggs, put the flowers, put the pen into, wipe the desktop, fold the clothes, pick up garbage, open the drawer. Columns are consecutive time steps from left to right. They show the scene's initial state, the black robot arm and gripper approaching and manipulating objects, and the final completed state. Most rows use a top-down view of a white table with small objects: plush toys, eggs, a rose, pens, a green cloth. The last two rows show a carpeted floor with a trash can and a drawer cabinet. There are no arrows, diagrams or equations, so the eye goes to the varied photographs.
caption: Cross-scene zero-shot real-robot deployment. We deploy SimVLA without any additional fine-tuning on held-out scenes and evaluate it on multi-stage tasks (e.g., store dolls, arrange eggs, fold clothes) that require both dexterous manipulation and semantic understanding.
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models often bundle architectural changes with different pretraining data, backbone scales, and optimization recipes, obscuring what actually drives progress. We introduce SimVLA, a deliberately minimal VLA, a standard vision-language backbone with a lightweight continuous-action head, as a controlled testbed for this attribution problem; our contribution is methodological and empirical (a controlled attribution study and a minimal-baseline calibration), not a new technique. Across LIBERO, CALVIN, WidowX, and Google Robot, one-knob-at-a-time ablations show that training dynamics are the largest measured driver, producing performance swings of $Î$$\approx$54--94\%, while task configuration and architecture have smaller effects under matched settings. Despite using a small backbone and no additional large-scale robot-data VLA pretraining before benchmark-specific training, SimVLA reaches 98.6\% average success on LIBERO, remains competitive across the other benchmarks, and transfers to held-out real-robot scenes. These results suggest that simple, carefully controlled VLA baselines remain underexplored and provide a calibration point for future architectural claims within the VLM-encoder plus lightweight-head family. Website: https://frontierrobo.github.io/SimVLA
